## What the model says

The memory measurement model (M3; [Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000159)),
implemented in the R package bmm, treats recall as a choice among response candidates, the options a
participant can give. Each candidate has an activation, how strongly it comes to mind, and candidates
with the same sources of activation form a category. In a simple-span task (bmm's version `ss`) there
are three categories: the item at the cued position (`corr`), the other list items (`other`), and
candidates that were not on the list (`npl`, not-presented lures). A complex-span task (version `cs`)
adds distractors, items processed between the list items, in two more categories: distractors in or
close to the cued position (`dist_context`) and the other distractors (`dist_other`). The activations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_\text{corr} &= b + a + c & A_\text{dist\_context} &= b + f \cdot a + f \cdot c \\
A_\text{other} &= b + a & A_\text{dist\_other} &= b + f \cdot a \\
A_\text{npl} &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

with background activation `b`, general activation `a`, context activation `c` and, in complex span,
filtering `f` between 0 and 1. A choice rule turns the activations into the probability $p_i$ that a
response falls in category $i$; bmm offers three, which are different models of that step. Each category is weighted by its number of candidates $n_i$
(`num_options` in bmm), and $j$ runs over the categories:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{simple:}&\quad p_i = \frac{n_i A_i}{\sum_j n_j A_j} \\[4pt]
\text{softmax:}&\quad p_i = \frac{n_i e^{A_i}}{\sum_j n_j e^{A_j}} \\[4pt]
\text{gaussian:}&\quad p_i = n_i \int \phi(z)\, \Phi(z)^{n_i - 1} \prod_{j \neq i} \Phi(z + A_i - A_j)^{n_j}\, dz
\end{aligned}
$$

Under the gaussian rule every candidate's activation gets independent standard normal noise and the
largest value is recalled; $\phi$ and $\Phi$ are the standard normal density and distribution
function. bmm computes the integral with 40-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and this page uses bmm's
nodes. Only the ratios of activations matter under the simple rule, and only their differences
under softmax and gaussian, so one activation has to set the scale: bmm fixes `b` at 0.1 under the
simple rule and at 0 under the other two. `a` reaches every
item on the studied list, `c` comes from the cue and reaches only the item at the cued position, and
`f` scales both for the distractors.

## The task

One trial is cued recall from a candidate set. A list of letters is studied one at a time; then one
box is cued with a question mark, and the participant picks the letter that was in it from the
candidates on the screen. The candidates are the correct letter (blue), the other letters of the list
(orange) and letters that were not on the list (grey). Slots marked xxx are not in use on this trial.
Set size is the number of letters studied; `n_other` of the other list letters are offered at test,
so `n_other` is at most set size − 1. N is the total number of candidates.

In the complex-span version a distractor letter follows each list letter (dashed tiles); it is read
aloud and not to be remembered. Which distractors count as close to the cued position is left to the
design: `m3()` takes only the number of candidates in each category, however the design assigned
them. The assignment here is this page's choice. It cues the third letter (the last one in a shorter
list) and counts the distractor just after it and the one just before it as close in context (green),
the others as not (purple). At set size 1 the cued letter is the first, with no distractor before it,
so only one distractor is close. `n_dist_context` of the close and `n_dist_other` of the other
distractors are offered at test. Set size goes up to 6 and lures up to 9 there, so that every
candidate fits on the screen.

## Explore

Each bar is the probability of a response in that category; the bars sum to 1. Raising `a` lifts every
list item and, by $f \cdot a$, every distractor, so the lures lose responses. Raising `c` lifts the
correct item: P(correct) rises, and other list items, lures and far distractors lose. In complex span
the near distractors gain $f \cdot c$ as well, and their share can rise or fall. Raising `f` moves the
near distractors' activation from a lure's (`b`, at `f` = 0) toward the correct item's (`b + a + c`, at
`f` = 1), and the far distractors' toward another list item's (`b + a`). With positive `a` and `c` the
distractors together then draw more responses, though one distractor category alone can lose some to
the other. Set size alone does not move the bars (see below). Reset returns the
parameters to the current rule's prior means and the task settings to their starting values.

Slider ranges come from bmm's default priors. The simple rule estimates log `a` with
normal(0, 1) and log `c` with normal(3, 1); softmax estimates `a` and `c` directly with normal(3, 1),
gaussian with normal(2, 1). Each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD: under the simple rule `a` runs
from 0.05 to 20 and `c` from 1 to 403, under softmax both run from 0 to 6, under gaussian from −1
to 5. `f` is estimated on the logit scale with a logistic(0, 1) prior, whose SD is π/√3 ≈ 1.81, so its
slider runs from 0.004 to 0.996 and starts at 0.5. The sliders start at the prior means (dashed). Switching the rule
restarts `a` and `c` there; the same number means something else under each rule.

## Across task settings

The counts $n_i$ enter the probabilities $p_i$, and through them the likelihood (the probability the
model assigns to the observed responses). The model therefore predicts how recall changes with the
size of the response set without a new parameter: the parameters stay as set; only the counts
change. Every added candidate competes with the correct one, so P(correct) falls as N grows. Other
list items have activation `b + a`, so for positive `a` they compete harder than lures, which have
only `b`. Distractors far from the cue have `b + f a`: with `f` near 0 they compete like lures, with
`f` near 1 like other list items. Under the simple and softmax rules a count multiplies its
category's weight; under the gaussian rule a category with $n$ candidates competes through the
largest of $n$ noisy values, so the same added candidates lower P(correct) along a different curve.
<span id="m3-across-now"></span> These numbers follow the controls.

Set size is not in the likelihood of either version. It limits how many list items and distractors
can be offered, and only those counts enter. A longer list with the same response set predicts the
same proportions unless the bmm formula lets the parameters differ between set sizes.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="m3-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="m3-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/m3.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `m3()` defines the model (`version = "ss"` for simple span,
`"cs"` for complex span), `dm3()` returns the log probability of a set of response counts, and
`bmf()` writes the formula for `bmm()`, which estimates `a`, `c` and, in complex span, `f` from data;
`my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms. `b` is not passed: bmm adds
it from the choice rule. In the complex-span code the distractor categories are called `distcontext`
and `distother`: bmm turns category names into brms parameter names, which cannot contain
underscores. See the [M3 article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_m3.html) for the
full model, including custom activation functions, and the reference pages for
[`m3()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/m3.html) and
[`dm3()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/m3dist.html).
